sentences.text: Alnashetri was a tiny, non-avian coelurosaur dinosaur that stood only 35 centimeters tall and measured 60 centimeters in length.
Its common name translates to "slender thighs," a reference to the animal's exceptionally long and thin hind legs.
This creature holds the record for being the smallest alvarezsauroid discovered to date.
The original discovery included a specimen with hind limbs that were perfectly connected to each other.
Scientists Peter J. Makovicky, Sebastián Apesteguía, and Federico A. Gianechini first named this extinct theropod in 2012.
A more complete skeleton was unearthed in 2014 and officially described in 2026, while another new specimen was reported by the same team in 2026.
The specific name cerropoliciensis honors the village of Cerro Policía, which assisted researchers after the site was found in 1999.
The holotype specimen preserves a partial left femur, the lower sections of both tibiae, a right fibula, and various foot bones.
A more complete skeleton, cataloged as MPCA Pv377, was determined to belong to a female individual.
Early phylogenetic work placed this animal within the superfamily Alvarezsauroidea.
Subsequent research recovered it as a basal member of the family Alvarezsauridae, positioned more advanced than Xiyunykus and Bannykus.
As a member of the Alvarezsauridae family, Alnashetri is classified broadly as a reptile.
Fossils were recovered from red sandstones in the upper Candeleros Formation near the boundary with the Huincul Formation.
The animal lived during the Albian stage, approximately 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago.
Some experts question the reliability of evidence placing Alnashetri in Alvarezsauroidea, noting that heavy reliance on ankle anatomy might yield false results.
Because the original skeleton is fragmentary, the species lacks specific shared traits needed for a precise assignment to a ceratosaurian group.
